title: Memory Hierarchy
description: Explore the tradeoff between speed and size across registers, caches, RAM, and disk, and understand why this hierarchy is the backbone of every performance optimization.

segments.text: Here's a fundamental truth of computing: fast memory is small and expensive, large memory is slow and cheap. Every system you'll ever design lives within this constraint. Let's explore why.
At the very top: registers. These live inside the CPU itself. A modern processor has maybe a few dozen registers, each holding sixty-four bits. Access time? Under one nanosecond. Essentially instant.
Next: L1 cache. About sixty-four kilobytes per core, split between data and instructions. Access takes roughly one nanosecond. It's tiny, but the CPU checks here first for almost everything.

L2 cache sits at about two hundred fifty-six kilobytes to one megabyte, taking around four nanoseconds. L3 is shared across cores, often thirty megabytes or more, at roughly ten nanoseconds. Each level trades speed for size.

Then we hit main memory, RAM. Sixteen to sixty-four gigabytes typically. Access takes about one hundred nanoseconds. That's a hundred times slower than L1 cache. When people say 'memory is fast,' they've never compared it to cache.
Notice the pattern? Each level is roughly ten times larger and ten times slower. This isn't a coincidence. It's physics and economics working together.
segments.thought_prompt: Why can't we just make all memory as fast as L1 cache?

segments.text: Below RAM: SSDs. Hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes. Access latency is around one hundred microseconds, a thousand times slower than RAM. But SSDs are non-volatile. Power goes off, your data survives.

At the bottom: hard disk drives. Terabytes of space, but access takes roughly ten milliseconds. That's ten million nanoseconds. Compared to an L1 cache hit, reading from a spinning disk is like walking to the moon.

This hierarchy only works because of locality. Temporal locality: data you accessed recently you'll likely access again. Spatial locality: data near what you accessed is likely needed next. Caches exploit both of these.

When the data you need isn't in cache, that's a cache miss. The CPU stalls while it fetches from a slower level. A program with poor locality can run ten times slower than one with good locality, on the same hardware.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you structure a large array traversal to maximize cache hits?

segments.text: This is why iterating a two-dimensional array row by row is dramatically faster than column by column. Row-major order means consecutive elements sit next to each other in memory. The cache loves it.

Remember this hierarchy: registers, L1, L2, L3, RAM, SSD, HDD. Each level bigger and slower. Every performance bottleneck in system design traces back to this pyramid. Understand it, and you understand half of all optimization.
